title: Attention residue
hook: part of the mind stays on the last task after the switch (Leroy)

segments.voice: Yesterday, switching costs: each change of task charges a little time and accuracy. Your line was one at a time.

The meeting ended ten minutes ago. The body has moved on: new room, new screen, new task. But a sentence from the meeting is still playing. What did she mean by that? Should I have said something? The report in front of you gets read, and read again, and nothing goes in. Part of the mind didn't get the memo that it moved. A researcher named Sophie Leroy gave that leftover a name, and it's today's word.
screen: `THE MEETING IS OVER.` → `THE SENTENCE IS STILL PLAYING.` → `THE REPORT WON'T GO IN.`

segments.voice: First, the finding. Leroy studied what happens when people leave one task and start another. Thoughts about the first task kept running in the background, and people with more of those leftover thoughts did worse on the next task. She called it attention residue: some of your attention stays stuck to the thing you just left. Second, what makes it stickier. In her studies, residue was stronger when the first task was left unfinished. A half-done job keeps tapping on the shoulder. When people finished it, especially under a little time pressure that pushed them to close it out, the residue was lower. Third, a way to loosen it. In later work, Leroy and a colleague tested something simple: before switching, people wrote a quick plan for where they would pick the task back up. That small note seemed to help the mind let go, as if it trusted the plan to remember so it didn't have to. Fourth, an old echo. The Stoic emperor Marcus Aurelius, in his private notebook, kept urging himself to give full attention to the thing in hand and to set aside every other thought while doing it. He had no lab and no word for residue, but he knew the problem: the mind trailing behind the body, still in the last room. The research doesn't say you can switch with no leftover. It suggests the leftover can shrink, by finishing what you can and writing down what you can't.
screen: `THE LAST TASK KEEPS RUNNING.` · `UNFINISHED WORK STICKS HARDER.` · then, large: `WRITE WHERE YOU'LL PICK IT UP.` · then: `THE THING IN HAND.`

segments.voice: Bring back whatever you were doing just before this, and if it's unfinished, say silently in one short sentence where you'll pick it up: next I'll call the landlord, next I'll fix page three. That's the note, so set it down and let the breath be the new room you've walked into. When the last task tugs, don't fight it; remind yourself the note has it, and come back.
Attention residue. The part of the mind that stays on the last task after you've moved to the next one. Today's word.
Your line: clear the residue. The note remembers, so the mind can let go. Day twelve seventy-three.

howItsDone: People who use this research often close each task with a short note on where to resume, or take a brief pause between meetings before starting the next thing.

chat.says: I finished the meeting but can't focus on this report. Why's my head still back there?
options: That's attention residue. Unfinished tasks stick; a quick note on where to resume can help.
It means you switched too slowly; faster switches leave no leftover thoughts.
That only happens when a meeting went badly, never after a good one.
chat.meaning: Leroy found thoughts about a left task keep running and hurt the next one, more so when it's unfinished. Writing where you'll pick it up seemed to help.
